question.explanation:
The denominator is $3 + 10\textrm{i}$ and its conjugate is $3 - 10\textrm{i}.$ We multiply both the numerator and the denominator by $3 - 10\textrm{i},$ so that the denominator turns into a real number:

\begin{eqnarray} \eqalign{ \dfrac {6} {3 + 10\textrm{i}} &= \dfrac {6} {3 + 10\textrm{i}}\cdot \dfrac {3 - 10\textrm{i}} {3 - 10\textrm{i}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {18 - 60\textrm{i}} {9 -30\textrm{i}+30\textrm{i}-10^2\textrm{i}^2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {18 - 60\textrm{i}} {9 - 100\textrm{i}^2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {18 - 60\textrm{i}} {9-100(-1)} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {18 - 60\textrm{i}} {9+100} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {18 - 60\textrm{i}} {109} \\ } \end{eqnarray}

Now that the denominator is a real number, we can write the complex number in the form $a+b \textrm{i}\mathbin{:}$

\begin{eqnarray} \eqalign{ \dfrac {18 - 60\textrm{i}} {109} = \dfrac{18}{109} - \dfrac{60}{109}\textrm{i} } \end{eqnarray}

example.title: Dividing a Real Number by a Complex Number

question.explanation:
The denominator is $-4 + 3\textrm{i}$ and its conjugate is $-4 - 3\textrm{i}.$ We multiply both the numerator and the denominator by $-4 - 3\textrm{i},$ so that the denominator turns into a real number:

\begin{eqnarray} \eqalign{ \dfrac {\phantom{,}8\textrm{i}} {-4 + 3\textrm{i}} &= \dfrac {\phantom{,}8\textrm{i}} {-4 + 3\textrm{i}} \cdot\dfrac {-4 - 3\textrm{i}} {-4 - 3\textrm{i}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {-32\textrm{i} - 24\textrm{i}^2} {(-4)^2 - 3^2\textrm i^2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {-32\textrm{i} - 24(-1)} {(-4)^2 - 3^2(-1)} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {-32\textrm{i} +24} {16 + 9} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {24-32\textrm{i} } {25} } \end{eqnarray}

Now that the denominator is a real number, we can write the complex number in the form $a+b \textrm{i}\mathbin{:}$

\begin{eqnarray} \eqalign{ \dfrac {24-32\textrm{i} } {25}= \dfrac {24} {25} - \dfrac {32} {25}\textrm{i} } \end{eqnarray}

example.title: Dividing an Imaginary Number by a Complex Number

question.explanation:
Here, the denominator is the imaginary number $10\textrm{i}.$ Note that this can be written as $0+10\textrm{i},$ so the conjugate is $0-10\textrm{i},$ or simply $-10\textrm{i}.$

So, we multiply both the numerator and the denominator by $-10\textrm{i},$ so that the denominator turns into a real number:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{-7+6\textrm{i}}{10\textrm{i}} &= \dfrac{-7+6\textrm{i}}{10\textrm{i}} \cdot \dfrac {-10\textrm{i}} {-10\textrm{i}}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac {70\textrm{i} - 60\textrm{i}^2} {-100\textrm{i}^2}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac {70\textrm{i} - 60(-1)} {-100(-1)}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac {60 +70\textrm{i}} {100} \end{align*}

Now that the denominator is a real number, we can write the complex number in the form $a+b \textrm{i}\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac {60 +70\textrm{i}} {100} &= \dfrac{60} {100} + \dfrac{70}{100}\textrm{i} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3} {5} + \dfrac{7}{10}\textrm{i} \end{align*}
